name: secretless-connector
context: An application must authenticate to a database, broker, or HTTP service, but the credential must not exist inside the application process. The app is a third-party image you cannot rebuild, it is scaled horizontally so a mounted secret is copied everywhere, its environment is captured by crash dumps and monitoring agents, and rotating the credential currently means redeploying every instance. The secretless connector changes the topology instead of the code: a broker runs alongside the workload, the application is told to connect to localhost or a Unix socket, and the broker performs the authentication phase of the target protocol on the application's behalf before piping the data-transfer phase through unmodified. Credentials live only inside the broker process and are re-fetched on each new connection.
benefits: The client never handles the credential. The broker intercepts the connection, completes the target's authentication handshake, and the protocol's data phases are a direct pass-through, so the application's connection code stays a plain host-and-port and no vault SDK is required
The application's credential-handling code disappears entirely, along with its own cache-expiry, token-renewal and vault-unavailable failure modes
Rotation is invisible to the application: when a secret changes manually or through a rotator, the broker obtains the new one the next time it opens a connection, with no restart and no redeploy

The broker authenticates to the vault using its own identity - a vault token, a Conjur host identity, a Kubernetes ServiceAccount, or a mounted secret - so the application's own credential surface is minimal and platform-issued
It works for arbitrary legacy clients because it operates on the wire rather than through an SDK. No modification to the application is needed, only a changed connection address
Local-only exposure: the broker listens on a Unix socket or 127.0.0.1, so the credential path never crosses a network and is not reachable from another pod
tradeoffs: Another process and another hop in the critical path. If the broker is not scheduled, or its vault credential is invalid, the application cannot open any connection to the backend - the failure is total for that workload
The broker is a concentration of privilege: it holds every credential the pod needs, so a broker compromise is a compromise of everything that pod can reach, not one of them
Coverage is finite. There is one Service Connector per supported protocol and one Secret Provider per supported vault, so an unsupported backend simply cannot use the pattern

Protocol awareness is the price of injection. The broker must implement the target's authentication handshake, and it must be updated if the target ever changes it - this is maintenance, not a one-time integration
Connection semantics change: unless the broker caches credentials per target, every new connection triggers a credential fetch, which adds latency and load on the vault
The credential problem is moved, not solved, for the broker itself. Its configuration file contains provider credentials and CA material, so a new secret to protect replaces the old one
Readiness and liveness must account for the broker, so an app that reports healthy with a dead broker still fails every request
use_cases: A vendor application image that cannot be rebuilt to fetch credentials from a vault
A legacy service whose connection code hardcodes a username and password and whose rotation procedure is a redeploy
Concentrating backend credentials so a container escape yields a socket rather than a password
Rolled-back or replicated deployments that otherwise each carry their own copy of the credential
avoid_when: The runtime cannot host a sidecar - strict FaaS with no long-lived companion process removes the pattern's placement
The backend protocol has no connector and cannot be tunnelled behind a supported one
Per-connection credential fetch would exceed the vault's capacity at the workload's connection rate and no caching policy is possible
The pod's blast radius is not isolated - if the pod already holds broad authority, brokering credentials adds little
Availability of the credential path is not the top concern and the extra hop is pure cost
anti_patterns: Deploying one centrally shared broker for many workloads instead of a per-workload sidecar, which concentrates every credential in a single blast radius
Leaving the real credential in the application's environment variables as a 'fallback', which defeats the whole point of the pattern
Exposing the broker on a routable address rather than a Unix socket or loopback, so the credential-brokering endpoint becomes network reachable
Assuming rotation is free: the broker re-authenticates when it opens a connection, so long-lived pooled connections keep presenting the old credential until they are recycled
Storing the broker's own vault token inside the image or a ConfigMap, deferring secret zero instead of solving it
Running the broker as a shared cluster service when the target namespace scoping of secrets is the isolation property you actually wanted
design_principles: Never let the credential enter the process that does not need it
Complete the target protocol's authentication where the credential lives, and leave the data path untouched
Place the broker on the same trust boundary as the workload so the credential never crosses a network
Make rotation a property of the connection, so it is invisible to the client
One broker per workload, so isolation is the default and not an exception
best_practices: Deploy as a sidecar in the same pod, bound to a Unix socket or 127.0.0.1, with the application container's connection address rewritten to localhost
Authenticate the broker to the vault with a platform identity (ServiceAccount, host identity) rather than a stored vault token
Cache credentials per target service so connection churn does not translate into vault load
Include the broker in readiness checks so the pod does not report healthy with a dead broker
Keep the broker's own configuration in a mounted ConfigMap and its CA material in a properly scoped secret
Remove the application's credential-fetch code entirely after the broker is in place - a leftover fallback path is the usual way this pattern fails in practice
